newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM vows to wipe out perk abuses.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM vows to wipe out perk abuses.

text.p: A key Australian senator being investigated by police for abusing expenses was in hospital on Friday suffering from a mystery illness as Prime Minister John Howard pledged to stamp out parliamentary corruption.

Howard, whose public support has fallen during a two-month scandal over expense abuses or rorts, sought to reassure voters over the honesty of their politicians and said he would tighten controls over MPs' perks.
"I am quite serious about devising a system that is as rort-proof as possible," Howard said in a television interview.
"Ninety-nine percent of members of parliament on both sides are very honest, hard-working men and women."
Senator Mal Colston, an independent who is also deputy president of the upper house, was admitted to a hospital in his home city of Brisbane late on Thursday.

Howard this week called in the federal police to investigate Colson after an employee of the senator went back on a previous statement that her sloppy book-keeping was to blame for his over-claiming 43 nights of travel allowance. Colston
Colston faces a wide range of other allegations, but has denied any wrongdoing.

Howard said he expected Colston, whose vote in the upper house has been crucial to government legislation, to stand down as Senate deputy president before the upper house resumes on May 6, or be forced out.
"I am sure he'll be gone as deputy president before the Senate resumes, and if he's not, we'll vote him out," he said.
Senate president Margaret Reid returned to Canberra after cutting short an overseas trip because of the scandal and urged Colston to stand aside as her deputy in running the chamber.
A spokesman for Brisbane's Wesley hospital said Colston was comfortable, but would not say what the corpulent Queensland senator was suffering from.
"He's been admitted with a medical condition and he's resting comfortably," said spokesman Ray Crompton.

The Labor opposition and key Senate minority parties have demanded Colston quit the Senate altogether, a move that would threaten future government measures including the 1997/98 budget due to be unveiled on May 13.

Colston was a Labor senator until he defected to sit as an independent last year. If forced out by political pressure or a fraud conviction he would be replaced by a Labor politician without a by-election being held.
Howard's year-old government does not have a majority in the upper house and has relied on support from Colston and another independent to pass key measures, including budget cuts.
The government, which pledged new ethical standards when it swept to power after 13 years in opposition, has been rocked by a widening scandal over alleged perks abuses.

Attorney-General Daryl Williams said on Tuesday a government backbencher and a recently-retired senate colleague would be charged with fraud over travel and car entitlements after police investigated boty men.
But the government has suffered more political damage from the Colston affair because of its support for his election as deputy president, a post which brings extra pay and benefits.
